Eschew
es-CHOO
verb
From Old French eschiver, “to shun, avoid, flee from,” itself from a Frankish/Old High German root skiuhan, to dread or shrink from (the same root that gives modern shy and shun). In the KJV it renders Hebrew sūr (to turn aside, depart from) and Greek ekklinō (to turn away from).

Biblical Definition

To eschew is to turn aside from, to shun, to shrink away from as from a loathed thing—a stronger word than merely to avoid, for it carries the recoil of dread. It is the settled verb of Job’s character: that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil (Job 1:1), and twice the LORD Himself repeats the commendation to Satan—a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil (Job 1:8; 2:3). The pairing is exact and instructive: the fear of God and the eschewing of evil rise and fall together, for reverence toward the Holy One breeds recoil from what He hates. Job does not merely refrain from evil as one who calculates its costs; he shrinks from it as one who loves God shrinks from what would grieve Him. Peter gathers the same posture into the imperative of the whole Christian walk: Let him eschew evil, and do good; let him seek peace, and ensue it (1Pe 3:11)—a turning from and a turning toward, a fleeing and a following. To eschew is thus the negative side of holiness, inseparable from its positive side: the same fear that makes a man depart from iniquity makes him pursue righteousness. Where the fear of God is lost, the recoil from evil is lost with it, and men grow bold in the very things from which the upright shrink.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ESCHEW as to flee from; to shun; to avoid, as something wrong, hurtful, or disgusting.

expand to see more

ESCHEW, v.t. — To flee from; to shun; to seek to avoid; to keep at a distance from, as from something evil, hurtful, or offensive. One that feared God, and eschewed evil (Job 1:1).

ESCHEW, v.t. — To decline; to abstain from; to have nothing to do with, from a settled aversion of the mind.

ESCHEW, v.t. — To turn aside from a course or thing, as one shrinks from what he dreads or abhors.

ESCHEWER, n. — One who shuns or avoids; one who habitually turns from what is evil.

ESCHEWING, ppr. — Shunning; avoiding; fleeing from; declining, as from a thing dreaded or abhorred.

Key Scripture

Job 1:1 — "There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil."

Job 1:8 — "And the LORD said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil?"

Job 2:3 — "And the LORD said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil? and still he holdeth fast his integrity, although thou movedst me against him, to destroy him without cause."

1Pe 3:11 — "Let him eschew evil, and do good; let him seek peace, and ensue it."

Modern Corruption

Not a doctrine under dispute but a lost strength of aversion; it recovers the recoil from evil that the fear of God breeds, in an age that has taught men to tolerate, explore, and be curious about what the upright shrink from.

expand to see more

The temper of the age is precisely the opposite of eschewing. Where Job shrank from evil as from a loathed thing, the modern conscience is trained to be broad-minded toward it, to explore it, to withhold judgment, to call recoil itself a kind of narrowness. The very reflex of dread before sin—the flinching of a heart that fears God—is dismissed as squeamishness or hate. But Scripture ties the two together and will not let them part: one that feared God, and eschewed evil. Lose the fear of God and the eschewing goes with it; men grow easy and curious and at last companionable with the things from which the holy shrink. The word rebukes the flattering counsel that a mature faith must lose its recoil; it insists rather that the more a man loves the Holy One, the more violently he turns from what would grieve Him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the unbreakable link between reverence and aversion. To fear God is to hate what He hates, and to hate evil is to eschew it—to turn aside, to shun, to shrink away—not merely to refrain when it is costly. Peter joins the negative to the positive: eschew evil, and do good; seek peace, and ensue it. Holiness is this double motion, a fleeing and a following, and the man who has lost the flee will soon lose the follow. Cultivate again the tender conscience that recoils; it is not weakness but the fear of God made visible in a life.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French eschiver / Frankish skiuhan (to dread, shrink from) — to shun, flee from; rendering Hebrew sūr (turn aside) and Greek ekklinō, the recoil of a God-fearing heart from evil.

expand to see more

Old French eschiver — to shun, avoid, flee from; the immediate source of the English verb.

Frankish / Old High German skiuhan — to dread, shrink back; the same root behind modern shy and shun.

Hebrew sūr (H5493) — to turn aside, depart, remove; used of departing from evil (Job 1:1; Pro 3:7; 16:6).

Greek ekklinō (G1578) — to turn away from, avoid, eschew (1Pe 3:11; Rom 3:12; 16:17).

English shy, shun — the surviving native cousins of the same Germanic root, keeping the sense of shrinking away.

Usage

"One that feared God, and eschewed evil—the two clauses are one character; the reverence and the recoil cannot be separated in an upright man."

"Peter’s double command: eschew evil, and do good; seek peace, and ensue it—a turning from and a turning toward, the whole motion of the sanctified life."

"The age counsels tolerance and curiosity where Scripture counsels eschewing; the tender conscience that shrinks from evil is not narrowness but the fear of God made visible."
